case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the U.S. Supreme Court may (and should) vacate an Oklahoma capital conviction and death sentence in a state postconviction posture when the State’s chief prosecutor effectively confesses that the prosecution presented false/misleading testimony and suppressed or failed to correct material impeachment evidence, but the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals refused relief under its own prejudice/harmless-error analysis.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause (Brady v. Maryland disclosure duties; Napue v. Illinois/Giglio v. United States duty to correct false testimony) and the Supreme Court’s appellate review authority over final state judgments under 28 U.S.C. § 1257.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Glossip argues that his conviction and death sentence rest on constitutionally unreliable proceedings because the prosecution’s case turned on accomplice Justin Sneed’s testimony and the State failed to disclose and/or failed to correct material information undermining Sneed’s credibility and the prosecution’s theory. He contends that under clearly established due process principles (Brady/Napue/Giglio), the suppressed or uncorrected evidence was material because the jury’s decision depended heavily on Sneed and because the withheld information would have substantially changed how the jury assessed motive, credibility, and the alleged solicitation-for-hire narrative. Glossip further argues that the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals applied an unduly demanding prejudice/harmless-error approach and that the Supreme Court can grant relief even in light of procedural complications because the federal constitutional violations go to the fundamental reliability of a capital conviction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Oklahoma argues that the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals’ judgment should stand because any alleged nondisclosure or misstatements were not material under the governing prejudice standards and therefore do not warrant vacatur in postconviction review. The State maintains that the conviction is supported by the overall evidentiary record (including corroborating circumstances and testimony beyond the challenged points), that the defense had substantial impeachment material already, and that the postconviction claims fail under independent state-law and/or federal harmless-error principles. Oklahoma (supported by states’ amicus briefing) also emphasizes institutional limits: a prosecutor’s “confession of error” does not automatically justify reversal; courts must independently determine whether a legal error occurred and whether it was prejudicial, particularly in final criminal judgments.
key_precedents: Grzegorczyk v. United States (statement respecting denial of certiorari by Justice Kavanaugh)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 1257 counsels restraint and that the OCCA may simply have made a record-bound materiality call—has force only if the state court genuinely applied Napue/Giglio’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard rather than an outcome-determinative prejudice/harmlessness test. But, as Justice Kagan emphasizes with Kyles and Wearry, when the State’s case turns on a cooperating accomplice, suppressed or uncorrected impeachment must be assessed cumulatively under the defendant-protective federal standard, and a state court cannot discount it as merely “cumulative” by effectively demanding that the verdict would have changed. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed narrow course is the institutional answer: vacate and remand for application of the correct federal materiality framework, without reweighing the whole trial ourselves or opining on broader state postconviction procedures. The prosecutor’s concession is not dispositive (as Alito notes), but it reinforces why a remand to apply the settled federal standards is appropriate to protect the trial’s truth-seeking function and the Court’s legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest contention—that the OCCA merely made a reasonable record-based call that the new impeachment was cumulative—still does not answer the federal question if the state court effectively required outcome-determinative prejudice rather than Napue/Giglio’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Bagley/Kyles treat constitutional materiality as the operative inquiry, and a state court may not insulate a due process violation by applying a more demanding harmlessness gloss once the prosecution has left false or misleading testimony uncorrected. Under a textualist/originalist view of the Fourteenth Amendment’s demand for fundamentally fair criminal process, credibility-driven capital cases are precisely where uncorrected falsity about the State’s key witness can reasonably affect the jury’s judgment even if some impeachment occurred. I therefore remain for vacatur and remand for application of the correct federal standard rather than deference to a materially different one.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Napue’s “reasonable likelihood” test is deliberately defendant-protective and that Kyles requires a cumulative view, but I remain unpersuaded that the OCCA actually substituted an outcome-determinative prejudice rule rather than applying the correct standard to a record it found already saturated with impeachment and corroboration. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Wearry and Banks underscores that impeachment can be material in an accomplice-driven case, yet those decisions involved markedly thinner corroboration and more stark credibility pivots than the OCCA reasonably identified here, so they do not compel the conclusion that the state court’s assessment conflicted with federal law. The prosecutor’s postconviction concession is relevant, but as I emphasized it cannot be allowed to function as a de facto per se Napue/Brady rule whenever additional impeachment emerges after trial. Given our limited role under § 1257, absent a clearer showing that the OCCA applied a categorically stricter legal standard (not merely reached a different materiality judgment), I would affirm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that the OCCA could be read as making a record-based materiality judgment—Sneed was already impeached and other evidence corroborated guilt—rather than adopting a categorically wrong rule. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Napue/Giglio’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard is intentionally defendant-protective, and a state court cannot effectively convert it into an outcome-determinative harmlessness inquiry by labeling new impeachment “cumulative,” especially in a credibility-driven capital case. Wearry and Banks underscore that when the prosecution’s narrative hinges on an accomplice, incremental impeachment and failure to correct misleading testimony can meaningfully alter the jury’s assessment, and Kyles requires considering the suppression’s cumulative effect on confidence in the verdict. The prosecutor’s concession is not controlling, but, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, it is powerful practical evidence that the truth-seeking function failed in a way due process cannot tolerate, warranting vacatur and remand for application of the correct federal standards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that the OCCA simply made a record-based call that the new impeachment was cumulative given existing attacks and corroboration—doesn’t fit the governing federal text and structure: Napue/Giglio ask whether there is any reasonable likelihood the falsity could have affected the jury, a deliberately defendant-protective standard that is triggered precisely when the State’s case hinges on an accomplice’s credibility. As the Chief Justice notes, Bagley/Kyles treat materiality as the constitutional prejudice inquiry itself, so a state court cannot effectively add an outcome-determinative harmlessness overlay by emphasizing that the verdict was otherwise “supported.” Wearry and Banks (raised by colleagues) reinforce that “already impeached” is not a talisman; incremental impeachment can still be material when it changes the narrative of why the key witness should be believed. The institutionally modest course, consistent with Justice Kavanaugh’s framing, is vacatur and remand for application of the correct Napue/Brady materiality standards to the whole record rather than our own reweighing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point—that the OCCA merely reached a record-based conclusion of immateriality given existing impeachment and corroboration—still runs into the governing federal text of Napue/Giglio: the question is whether there is any reasonable likelihood the uncorrected falsity could have affected the jury, not whether the remaining evidence could sustain the verdict. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that Bagley/Kyles require assessing suppressed impeachment cumulatively and that a state court may not effectively ratchet materiality into an outcome-determinative prejudice or add a second “harmless-error” screen once constitutional materiality is satisfied. Wearry and Banks (as Justice Kagan notes) underscore that “already impeached” is not a talisman; where the State’s case turns on a cooperating accomplice, incremental impeachment and the State’s failure to correct misleading testimony can readily meet Napue’s defendant-protective threshold. Section 1257 permits us to correct that misapplication of federal law on direct review, and the prosecutor’s concession—while not controlling—confirms rather than supplies the constitutional defect.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the institutional caution against reopening a final state capital judgment based on arguably cumulative impeachment, and his warning that we should not treat a prosecutor’s confession of error as dispositive. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Napue/Giglio’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard is intentionally more defendant-protective than an outcome-determinative prejudice or generic harmless-error framing, and a state court cannot effectively ratchet that standard up by leaning on “other impeachment” and “corroboration” to discount the incremental effect of uncorrected falsity. Kyles/Wearry matter here because they reinforce that cumulative impeachment—especially where the State’s case turns on an accomplice—can be material even if each piece looks “additional” in isolation, and we should not ourselves reweigh credibility on this record. The narrow, institutionally sound course is vacatur and remand for application of the settled federal standard, which answers Alito’s legitimacy concern without expanding the case into broader state postconviction issues.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is institutional: on § 1257 review we should not disturb a final state judgment based on mere disagreement with a record-specific materiality call, especially where the witness was already impeached and there is some corroboration. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Bagley and Kyles frame “materiality” as the constitutional prejudice inquiry itself, not a threshold after which a state court may effectively apply an additional harmless-error/outcome-determinative overlay; and Napue’s textually distinct “any reasonable likelihood” standard is deliberately defendant-protective. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Wearry and Banks reinforces that “cumulative impeachment” is not inherently immaterial where the State’s case turns on an accomplice’s credibility—precisely the circumstance in which even incremental corrections to misleading testimony can plausibly affect jurors’ assessment. On this record, the OCCA’s treatment of conceded falsity/suppression as merely cumulative reads like the stricter prejudice formulation Napue/Giglio forbid, so I remain for vacatur and remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest argument—that the OCCA simply made a record-based, deferential materiality call because Sneed was already impeached and some corroboration existed—does not answer the distinct federal question under Napue/Giglio: whether there is any reasonable likelihood the State’s uncorrected false or misleading testimony could have affected the jury’s judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Kyles requires assessing suppressed/uncorrected credibility evidence cumulatively, and a state court cannot effectively demand an outcome-determinative showing by labeling the new impeachment “merely cumulative” when the prosecution’s case hinged on a cooperating accomplice. Even if the prosecutor’s confession is not dispositive (as Justice Thomas notes), it is a practical indicator that the adversarial process did not function fairly here, and in a credibility-driven capital case that procedural defect readily undermines confidence in the verdict. The appropriate institutional course is a narrow vacatur and remand for application of the correct, defendant-protective Napue/Kyles framework rather than affirming on a de facto harmless-error rationale.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, we have authority to review and vacate a final state-court judgment that rests on an unreasonable application of clearly established federal due process rules governing suppression of material impeachment evidence and the State’s duty to correct false or misleading testimony. Napue v. Illinois and Giglio v. United States require relief where there is any reasonable likelihood the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment, and Bagley and Kyles make clear that this materiality inquiry effectively subsumes additional harmless-error review once a constitutional violation is found. Given the State’s chief prosecutor’s concession that key testimony was false/misleading and impeachment evidence was suppressed in a case hinging on an accomplice witness, the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals’ refusal to grant relief cannot be squared with those standards. A narrow disposition vacating the conviction and sentence and remanding for further proceedings best preserves institutional legitimacy by enforcing bedrock prosecutorial obligations without resolving broader questions of state postconviction procedure.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause forbids a State from obtaining a conviction through testimony it knows to be false or misleading and then leaving that falsehood uncorrected; under Napue v. Illinois and its progeny, relief is required when there is “any reasonable likelihood” the false testimony could have affected the jury’s judgment. That federal materiality rule is distinct from, and not satisfied by, a state court’s more demanding harmless-error or prejudice analysis; once a Napue violation is established, there is no additional harmless-error overlay beyond the constitutional materiality inquiry itself. Because Oklahoma’s postconviction disposition appears to apply a stricter prejudice/harmless-error approach than Napue permits in a case turning on an accomplice witness, the state judgment conflicts with controlling federal law, and this Court has authority under 28 U.S.C. § 1257 to vacate a final state judgment that violates federal due process. The prosecutor’s “confession of error” is not dispositive, but it underscores the due-process breach and the consequent unreliability of a capital conviction resting on uncorrected falsity and suppressed impeachment evidence (Giglio; Bagley; Kyles).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, this Court may review only federal questions decided by the state court, and it is not enough that a current prosecutor “confesses error” if the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals reasonably concluded the alleged Brady/Napue issues were not material under governing federal standards. Napue and Giglio require vacatur only when there is a “reasonable likelihood” the false or uncorrected testimony affected the verdict, and Brady/Bagley/Kyles require a showing of materiality in light of the entire record—not merely that additional impeachment would have been useful. Given the state court’s determination that the record contained substantial impeachment of Sneed already and other corroborating circumstances supporting guilt, I would defer to its judgment that any nondisclosure or misstatements did not undermine confidence in the outcome. Practical consequences also counsel restraint in upsetting a final capital judgment on postconviction review absent a clear, outcome-determinative due process violation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Due process forbids the State from obtaining a conviction through false or misleading testimony and imposes an affirmative duty to correct it; when such testimony goes uncorrected, relief is required if there is “any reasonable likelihood” it affected the jury’s judgment. Napue v. Illinois; Giglio v. United States. In a capital case that turns on an accomplice’s credibility, suppression of substantial impeachment material likewise violates Brady v. Maryland, and materiality must be assessed cumulatively under Kyles v. Whitley—not by an unduly demanding harmless-error lens that discounts the centrality of the tainted witness. This Court may review the OCCA’s federal due process determinations under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, and where the State’s chief prosecutor has effectively conceded the trial was infected by false/misleading testimony and suppressed impeachment evidence, vacatur is necessary to preserve the basic reliability of a death sentence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Fourteenth Amendment forbids the State from obtaining a conviction through false or misleading testimony it knows about or fails to correct, and Napue v. Illinois applies a comparatively defendant-protective materiality standard: whether there is any “reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment. Where, as here, the prosecution’s case substantially turned on an accomplice’s credibility, suppressed or uncorrected impeachment information goes to the heart of the truth-seeking function, and under Agurs/Bagley/Kyles there is no further harmless-error overlay once constitutional materiality is shown. The Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals’ refusal of relief—despite the State’s effective confession that critical testimony was false or misleading and impeachment material was withheld—reflects a prejudice/harmless-error approach more demanding than Napue permits, making the state judgment reviewable and reversible on federal due process grounds under 28 U.S.C. § 1257. A vacatur and remand best serves workability and coherence in the Brady/Napue/Giglio line, particularly in a capital case where reliability is paramount (cf. Wearry v. Cain; Banks v. Dretke).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, this Court may review and vacate a final state judgment that denies relief for a federal due process violation, and the Due Process Clause forbids the State’s knowing presentation of false or misleading testimony or its failure to correct it. Napue v. Illinois holds a conviction must be set aside when there is “any reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment, a standard especially implicated where the case turns on a single cooperating witness’s credibility. Separately, Brady v. Maryland and its progeny (including Bagley and Kyles) require disclosure of material impeachment evidence, assessed cumulatively, and a state court may not insulate a constitutional violation by applying a prejudice/harmless-error analysis more demanding than these federal standards. A prosecutor’s confession of error is not dispositive, but where the record shows a Napue/Brady violation meeting the governing materiality threshold, the Constitution requires vacatur and a new, reliable proceeding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1257, the Court has authority to review a final state judgment rejecting federal due process claims, and the prosecutor’s confession of error does not control but is relevant to whether Brady/Napue violations occurred. When the State knowingly presented or failed to correct false or misleading testimony, due process is violated if there is any “reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment, a stricter materiality standard than ordinary harmless-error review. Napue/Agurs and Bagley indicate that once that materiality threshold is met, there is no further harmless-error analysis to salvage the conviction, and in a capital case turning on an accomplice’s credibility, suppressed impeachment evidence can readily be material (see also Kyles and Wearry). Given the centrality of the key witness and the conceded suppression/misleading testimony, the Oklahoma court’s prejudice analysis appears inconsistent with these settled federal standards, warranting vacatur.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, a conviction obtained through the State’s uncorrected false or misleading testimony violates Napue v. Illinois and must be set aside if there is “any reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment, a standard reiterated in United States v. Agurs and distinct from more demanding harmless-error formulations. Given that the State’s case turned on accomplice testimony, suppressed or uncorrected impeachment bearing on that witness’s credibility is quintessentially material under Napue/Giglio and Brady’s materiality framework as explained in Bagley and Kyles, which assesses the cumulative effect on the verdict. Whatever deference is owed to the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals’ prejudice analysis, this Court has authority under 28 U.S.C. § 1257 to review and vacate a final state judgment that misapplies governing federal constitutional standards, and precedent like Wearry v. Cain underscores that even largely impeachment evidence can be material where the prosecution’s case is thin and credibility-driven. A prosecutor’s “confession of error” is not dispositive, but the Court must independently apply these federal standards, and on this record the due process violations undermine confidence in the reliability of a capital conviction and sentence.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Court has authority under 28 U.S.C. § 1257 to review final state judgments that turn on federal due process, and Brady/Napue/Giglio violations are quintessential federal questions bearing on the reliability of a capital conviction. Under Kyles v. Whitley and United States v. Bagley, materiality is assessed cumulatively and asks whether suppression undermines confidence in the verdict—not whether the defendant would more likely than not have been acquitted—an especially consequential standard where the State’s case hinges on an accomplice witness. If the State’s chief prosecutor concedes that the prosecution presented false or misleading testimony or failed to correct it (Napue v. Illinois) and also suppressed material impeachment evidence (Brady v. Maryland; Giglio v. United States), a state court cannot insulate the conviction by applying an unduly demanding prejudice/harmless-error approach inconsistent with these federal standards. Given the practical stakes in a death case and the centrality of credibility, due process requires vacatur and a new, procedurally fair proceeding.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Supreme Court may and should grant relief in a state capital case when the State’s chief prosecutor (the Oklahoma Attorney General) confesses that the conviction is legally unreliable, and whether the Oklahoma courts’ refusal to credit that confession rests on an erroneous view of federal law governing due process and false testimony.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause (as applied through doctrines barring convictions obtained via false testimony and/or suppression of material impeachment evidence—i.e., Napue/Giglio/Brady principles) and the Supreme Court’s certiorari authority to review state-court judgments that allegedly misapply those federal standards.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Glossip argues that his conviction and death sentence are constitutionally unreliable because they rested on a cooperating codefendant’s testimony (Justin Sneed) that is now conceded by the Oklahoma Attorney General to be infected by falsehoods and/or undisclosed impeachment material; he contends the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals applied the wrong federal standard (or applied it unreasonably) in rejecting relief even after the State’s confession of error, and that due process requires a new trial or other vacatur because the prosecution’s case depended on the credibility of the incentivized witness.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Oklahoma maintains that a state court is not bound to grant post-conviction relief merely because an executive official confesses error, that courts must independently determine whether a cognizable federal constitutional violation occurred, and that the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals reasonably concluded that any alleged falsehoods or nondisclosures were not material under governing due-process standards (and therefore do not justify overturning a final capital judgment).
key_precedents: Grzegorczyk v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2580 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., respecting denial of certiorari) (confession of error does not itself supply a legal basis to vacate)
Commonwealth v. Brown, 196 A.3d 130 (Pa. 2018) (state court independently reviews a prosecutor’s confession of error and requires a legal basis for relief)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that a confession of error cannot bind the judiciary and that we should not reweigh credibility or trial evidence simply because the executive has changed its mind; finality concerns carry real weight. But that argument does not resolve the narrower federal question, emphasized by Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh, whether the Oklahoma court applied Napue/Agurs’s “any reasonable likelihood” materiality standard or instead imported a more demanding Brady/Bagley-style prejudice inquiry when dealing with conceded falsity/withheld impeachment of a key witness. Justice Barrett’s adequate-and-independent-state-ground caution reinforces why our disposition must be tightly framed around the state court’s use (or misstatement) of the federal standard, not around the Attorney General’s concession. On that minimalist approach—vacate and remand for application of the correct Napue standard (with confession treated as evidence, not authority)—I remain with the Petitioner.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—confession of error is not binding and we should not reweigh trial evidence—does not resolve the dispositive issue identified by the Chief Justice: whether the Oklahoma court applied Napue/Agurs’s “any reasonable likelihood” test or instead a more demanding Brady/Bagley-style prejudice standard. If the state court treated conceded falsity or withheld impeachment of the prosecution’s key incentivized witness as immaterial by demanding a higher showing, that is a correctable error of federal law, and enforcing that settled rule does not expand due process beyond its original procedural guarantee against fundamentally unfair criminal process. Justice Barrett’s caution about adequate-and-independent state grounds underscores the need for a narrow holding, but it cuts in favor of focusing precisely on the state court’s articulation and application of the federal materiality standard, not on the Attorney General’s reassessment. On that limited ground—confession as evidence, not as authority—I remain with vacatur and remand to apply the correct Napue standard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point—that we are not bound by the Attorney General’s confession, but we must ensure the Oklahoma court did not smuggle in Brady/Bagley’s higher prejudice test instead of Napue/Agurs’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard. I agree that would be reversible federal-law error if clearly shown, but I do not read the state court’s decision (as characterized here) as a misstatement of the governing rule; it can fairly be understood as an application of materiality to the whole record, concluding the inaccuracies/impeachment would not have affected the verdict even under Napue’s more defense-protective standard. That is precisely the sort of fact-bound judgment we ordinarily do not second-guess on certiorari merely because the executive later reassesses the case, and finality concerns weigh especially heavily in capital litigation absent a clear constitutional misapplication. Justice Barrett’s separation-of-powers point reinforces that a confession of error is probative but not a substitute for identifying an actual Napue error by the state judiciary.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Barrett are right that an Attorney General’s confession of error cannot do the court’s work and that we should not reweigh the whole record, but that framing still leaves the controlling question: whether the Oklahoma court applied Napue/Agurs’s distinctly defense-protective “any reasonable likelihood” standard to the knowing use (or non-correction) of materially misleading testimony. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, where the State’s case depends on an incentivized cooperator, credibility impeachment is not “collateral”—it is often the fulcrum of guilt, and Napue’s lower materiality bar exists precisely to protect the trial’s truth-seeking function in that setting. If the state court effectively imported Brady/Bagley prejudice or discounted conceded falsity as mere impeachment, that is a misapplication of settled federal law we must correct, with particular force in a capital case where reliability and fairness for the vulnerable defendant are paramount. The confession is not dispositive, but it is probative corroboration that the jury may have been misled and that the due-process violation is not speculative.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point—that we cannot treat the Attorney General’s confession as dispositive and we must not reweigh the trial record—sets the right institutional boundary, but it doesn’t resolve the distinct question whether the Oklahoma court used the correct federal yardstick. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, if the OCCA effectively imported Brady/Bagley’s higher prejudice threshold (or otherwise discounted conceded falsity/impeachment about the central cooperator) rather than applying Napue/Agurs’s “any reasonable likelihood” test, that is a legal error we can correct without becoming a super-jury. Justice Barrett’s concern about the absence of a clear misstatement is serious, but the workability of Napue depends on courts treating credibility-taint in a credibility-driven case as material under its deliberately low standard; where the state court’s analysis reads as demanding more, vacatur and remand is the narrow, coherent remedy. The confession is evidence, not authority—but it strengthens the conclusion that the proceedings were constitutionally unreliable under settled due-process law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that an executive confession of error cannot bind the judiciary and that we should not redo a record-wide credibility assessment on certiorari; separation of powers demands an independent judicial application of the governing rule. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the decisive question is whether the Oklahoma court applied Napue/Agurs’s distinct “any reasonable likelihood” materiality standard (for known false or uncorrected misleading testimony) or effectively imported Brady/Bagley’s higher prejudice threshold—an error of federal law we are obliged to correct. Justice Barrett’s finality and adequate-and-independent-state-grounds concerns carry weight, yet finality cannot preserve a judgment resting on the wrong constitutional standard, and a narrow vacatur/remand to apply Napue properly does not convert the Attorney General’s view into a rule of decision. Absent clarity that the state court correctly used Napue’s standard, I remain persuaded the safer, more faithful course is to enforce that settled federal due-process rule and remand for proper application.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s finality/reweighing concern is serious, but it does not answer the narrow, reviewable question Chief Justice Roberts identifies: whether the Oklahoma court effectively applied a higher Brady/Bagley-like prejudice standard rather than Napue/Agurs’s deliberately lower “any reasonable likelihood” test in a credibility-driven case. Justice Barrett is right to insist that the Attorney General’s confession cannot do the judiciary’s work and that we must avoid converting executive reassessments into rules of decision; I would treat the confession only as corroborative context, not as dispositive authority. On the face of the state court’s reasoning, if it discounted conceded falsity/withheld impeachment about the key incentivized witness in a way inconsistent with Napue’s materiality framework, that is a federal-law misapplication we can correct without reweighing the entire record. A narrow vacatur/remand tied to the proper Napue standard preserves institutional legitimacy while enforcing settled due-process limits on convictions obtained through known false or misleading testimony.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the most serious point: if the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals truly imported Brady/Bagley’s higher prejudice threshold rather than applying Napue/Agurs’s “any reasonable likelihood” standard, that would be a correctable federal-law error. But Justice Alito is right that our role is not to reweigh the trial record or to treat the Attorney General’s confession as a rule of decision; absent a clear misstatement or unmistakable application of the wrong standard on the face of the opinion, I am reluctant to infer constitutional error from an arguably debatable materiality assessment. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on separation-of-powers principles (including the thrust of Grzegorczyk) reinforces my view that a confession of error is probative but cannot substitute for an independent judicial finding of a due-process violation. On this record as presented in conference, I do not yet see the kind of clear federal misapplication that warrants vacatur, especially given finality interests in a capital judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that we cannot treat the Attorney General’s confession as dispositive and should not reweigh the trial record—does not undermine my view because the decisive question is whether the Oklahoma court applied Napue/Agurs’s deliberately defendant-protective “any reasonable likelihood” standard or something closer to Brady/Bagley prejudice. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, enforcing the correct federal standard is not “reweighing”; it is ensuring the state court did not discount conceded falsity/withheld impeachment about a central incentivized witness in a way that effectively raises the materiality bar. Justice Barrett’s finality and restraint concerns are substantial, but they yield where the state court’s analysis appears to blur or heighten the governing Napue standard in a credibility-driven capital case, undermining procedural fairness and reliability. The appropriate, narrow remedy is vacatur and remand for application of the proper Napue framework, with the confession treated as probative but not controlling.

John Roberts.reasoning: A prosecutor’s confession of error is not itself a legal basis to vacate a conviction, but it is highly relevant insofar as it reflects the State’s acknowledgment of a federal due-process violation that the courts must assess independently. Under the Fourteenth Amendment, due process is violated when the prosecution knowingly allows false or misleading testimony to go uncorrected, and relief is required where there is any reasonable likelihood the false testimony could have affected the jury’s judgment—especially when, as here, the case hinges on the credibility of an incentivized cooperating witness. If the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals rejected relief by applying a more demanding materiality standard than Napue permits (or by treating the State’s admission as legally irrelevant to the Napue inquiry), that is an error of federal law warranting this Court’s intervention on narrow grounds. The appropriate remedy is a new trial (or equivalent vacatur) limited to correcting the identified due-process defect, preserving institutional legitimacy by enforcing settled precedent rather than expanding doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as this Court has long understood it, forbids a State from obtaining or maintaining a conviction through testimony the prosecution knows is false and fails to correct. Napue v. Illinois holds that a conviction must be set aside when there is “any reasonable likelihood” the false testimony could have affected the jury’s judgment, and Mooney v. Holohan likewise treats the knowing use of perjured testimony (and suppression of impeaching proof) as a due-process violation. Although a state court need not grant relief merely because an Attorney General confesses error, the confession here underscores that the record contains a federal constitutional violation under Napue/Giglio principles rather than a purely state-law claim. Because the prosecution’s case turned on the credibility of an incentivized witness and the State concedes uncorrected falsehoods and/or undisclosed impeachment, due process requires vacatur and a new trial.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A state court is not obliged to vacate a final conviction simply because the State’s Attorney General confesses error; the judiciary must independently determine whether a federal due-process violation occurred and whether it satisfies the governing materiality standard. Under Napue/Giglio, relief is warranted only if there is a “reasonable likelihood” that the challenged falsehood or nondisclosure could have affected the jury’s judgment, and the Oklahoma court could reasonably conclude that any inaccuracies or impeachment material were not material in light of the record as a whole. The Due Process Clause does not convert executive reassessments into binding legal determinations, and this Court’s certiorari review should not be used to reweigh credibility and trial evidence absent a clear misapplication of Napue/Giglio/Brady. Practical consequences also counsel restraint in overturning final state capital judgments without a demonstrated constitutional violation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Due Process Clause forbids a conviction obtained when the State knowingly uses or leaves uncorrected materially false or misleading testimony, including testimony going to credibility, and relief is required if there is any reasonable likelihood the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment. Napue v. Illinois makes clear that a prosecutor’s duty to correct false testimony is not diminished because the lie concerns only impeachment, and United States v. Agurs confirms the strict materiality standard where perjury corrupts the truth-seeking function of trial. In a capital case that turned on an incentivized cooperating witness, Oklahoma’s refusal to grant relief after the Attorney General’s concession—if premised on a higher materiality threshold or an unduly cramped view of Napue/Giglio/Brady—misapplies federal law and leaves an unreliable death judgment in place. While a confession of error is not itself dispositive, this Court may and should correct the state court’s erroneous application of due process and order a new trial or vacatur where the verdict’s reliability is constitutionally compromised.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A prosecutor’s confession of error is not itself a freestanding legal ground for vacatur, but it can underscore that the state court must correctly apply governing federal due-process standards when assessing alleged false testimony or suppressed impeachment evidence. Under Napue and its elaboration in Agurs, a conviction obtained through false testimony violates due process if there is "any reasonable likelihood" the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment—a particularly workable, credibility-centered inquiry when the State’s case turns on an incentivized cooperating witness. If the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals rejected relief by effectively demanding a more demanding showing than Napue/Giglio’s reasonable-likelihood materiality standard (or by discounting conceded falsity/withheld impeachment in a way incompatible with that standard), its judgment rests on an erroneous view of federal law reviewable under the Fourteenth Amendment. Given the centrality of Sneed’s credibility, the conceded unreliability is material under Napue’s framework, warranting at least a new trial.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A prosecutor’s confession of error cannot itself supply authority to vacate a final judgment, but it can be powerful evidence that a federal constitutional violation occurred; the question remains whether the conviction was obtained through false testimony or suppressed impeachment material in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. Under Napue v. Illinois and its progeny (as explained in United States v. Agurs), a conviction secured through the knowing use of false testimony must be set aside whenever there is any reasonable likelihood the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment—a stricter materiality standard than Brady/Bagley’s “reasonable probability.” Where the State’s case turns on an incentivized cooperating witness’s credibility, and the chief prosecutor concedes unreliability tied to falsehoods and/or undisclosed impeachment, the Oklahoma court’s refusal to apply Napue’s correct materiality rule rests on an erroneous view of federal law and cannot stand. Respect for separation of powers requires judicial independence from executive confessions, but it equally requires courts to enforce settled constitutional rules governing truthful evidence in criminal trials, especially in a capital case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A state attorney general’s confession of error is not itself a freestanding basis for vacatur, and a court must independently identify a federal constitutional violation. But under the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause, the knowing use of false testimony (or failure to correct it) requires relief if there is “any reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment, a stricter materiality standard than ordinary Brady/Bagley prejudice. If the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals effectively applied a more demanding standard (or treated the Attorney General’s concession as irrelevant to whether the State failed to correct material false testimony), that misapplication of Napue/Agurs warrants Supreme Court intervention and a new trial in a capital case where the prosecution hinged on an incentivized witness’s credibility. This approach respects finality and institutional limits while enforcing settled due-process precedent protecting the truth-seeking function of trial.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A state executive’s confession of error—while entitled to respect—does not itself supply the legal basis to vacate a final judgment; a court must independently determine whether a federal constitutional violation occurred. Under Napue v. Illinois and Agurs, due process is violated only if the State knowingly used false testimony and there is a “reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment; likewise, Brady/Giglio relief requires materiality. On this record, Oklahoma may reasonably argue that the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals’ refusal to treat the Attorney General’s position as binding and its conclusion that any alleged falsehoods or nondisclosures were not material under Napue/Brady reflect permissible application of federal standards rather than an error of federal law reviewable under 28 U.S.C. § 1257. Absent a clear misstatement of the governing federal materiality standard (or a judgment that turns on federal law rather than an adequate and independent state ground), this Court should not grant relief solely because the State’s chief prosecutor now doubts the conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Due process forbids a conviction obtained through the State’s knowing use of false testimony, and requires reversal where there is “any reasonable likelihood” the falsehood could have affected the jury’s judgment. Napue v. Illinois, 360 U.S. 264, 269–71 (1959). Here the State’s chief prosecutor concedes a Napue/Brady problem bearing directly on the credibility of the prosecution’s central, incentivized witness, so the practical consequences for reliability in a capital case strongly favor relief. While a confession of error alone does not supply an automatic basis to vacate (see Grzegorczyk v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2580 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., respecting denial of certiorari)), the Oklahoma court’s refusal to credit the conceded false-testimony/impeachment violations reflects an erroneous application of federal materiality under Napue’s lower “reasonable likelihood” standard, warranting this Court’s intervention under the Fourteenth Amendment.
